items.q: How does 'der Mann' change in the accusative case?
items.why: Students think English-style: objects are unchanged. German changes ARTICLES based on case. Masculine is the only gender that visibly changes in accusative: der to den. Feminine, neuter, and plural look the same.

items.q: How do you say 'I watch TV every evening' in German?
items.why: Students keep separable verbs together. FERNSEHEN splits in main clauses: sehe...fern. The prefix 'fern' goes to the END of the clause. Same with anrufen (rufe...an), aufstehen (stehe...auf), einkaufen (kaufe...ein).

A devastating faux ami. Bekommen looks like 'become' but means RECEIVE. 'Ich bekomme ein Geschenk' = I receive a present. To become = WERDEN. Confusion: 'I became a present' instead of 'I received a present'.

items.q: What is the correct reflexive pronoun: 'ich verstehe ___ gut mit meinen Eltern'?
items.why: The answer examiners want is: mich. “mir” is the distractor this question was built around — if it tempted you, that's the exact gap to close.

items.q: Up to how many months of Elterngeld can a couple receive (basic Elterngeld)?
items.why: Exact answer: 14 months. Estimation gets you near it; only the anchored number survives the exam hall.
